access_notes: Retrieved 2026-08-15 from Wikimedia Commons. EXIF: Samsung SM-G930V, 2018-07-24 09:32:25 local, 26 mm 35 mm-equivalent, f/1.7, 1/3225 s, ISO 50, orientation 1 (upright, unrotated). The camera's own timestamp corroborates the Commons DateTimeOriginal, which is what makes the July phenology first-hand rather than asserted.
note:
THE CALIBRATION REFERENCE. This is the photograph the renderer's sky is measured against - the file the world.js comments call 'bar/dupage_tallgrass_2018-07-24.jpg', which until now existed only in a working directory and in nobody's checkout. Committing it is what makes those numbers checkable.

Every figure world.js quotes was re-measured from THIS file on 2026-08-15 and reproduces (`python3 tools/measure_reference.py`). Sky/land step found per column by an 8-row luminance drop; median step row 820 of 3024. Band immediately above the step: measured sRGB (137,162,187) against the quoted (136,163,192). Sky by elevation, using the frame geometry below: 14.4 deg (97,151,208) against (101,153,209); 8 deg (119,163,206) against (125,165,205); 4 deg (133,166,201) against (137,166,200). The residual is a few units in red and blue, consistent with this re-measurement averaging the full frame width where the original sampled at the shot's own azimuth. Nothing in the renderer was changed to make them agree.

THE FRAME IS SOLVED, which is the part that outlives this record. The 26 mm equivalent gives a 53.1 deg vertical field over 3024 px = 57.0 px/deg, and the horizon sits at row 820, so the elevation of any pixel is (820 - row) / 57.0 degrees and the frame reaches 14.4 deg above the horizon and 38.7 deg below. That also lands the camera pitch at -12.1 deg, which was established independently by the 2026-08-10 prairie sweep as 'the reference photographer had tilted down ~12 deg' - two derivations of the same number that never saw each other.
what_it_supplies: the July clear-sky colour of this latitude by elevation, in sRGB, over 0-14.4 deg above the horizon - the anchor for SKY_EXPOSURE and HORIZON_RESTORE in renderers/web/js/world.js
the horizon-sky colour distance converges on, sRGB (136,163,192), which terrain.js and world.js both use as the haze target
a real July tallgrass sward at a known sun elevation, for tree-mass and ground contrast comparisons measured through the same code that measures a render (tools/critic_metrics.mjs)
a solved frame: 57.0 px/deg vertical, horizon at row 820, so any future measurement can state the elevation it was taken at instead of guessing
what_it_does_not_supply: the flower load of unmanaged 1835 prairie - it is a RESTORATION PLANTING on a former agricultural field, and seed mixes are bought for being forb-rich. This photograph must not be quoted for that number. R-W4c(b1) CORRECTED THIS ENTRY on 2026-08-15: it previously said 'the 2026-08-10 sweep measured 12.91 % here against 1.79-5.54 % on a never-plowed remnant, and the honest target is 4-6 %', and neither figure survives checking. 12.91 % does not reproduce - the committed recipe (tools/critic_metrics.mjs) reads 5.54 % on this frame, 7.02 % on its nearest quarter and 25.82 % with its two tests reordered - and NO never-plowed remnant photograph is committed to this repository, so 1.79-5.54 % cites nothing. That sentence was the only place in data/sources/ where the remnant appeared, which is how a target came to rest on a source that does not exist. There is no 4-6 % target; see docs/ROADMAP.md R-W4c(b1) and run tools/measure_bloom_target.mjs

an anti-sun sky. The frame looks within about 19 deg of the sun's azimuth, and world.js records that fitting an azimuth term needs a SECOND verified July photograph shot away from the sun. This file is not it
the species composition of 1835 Chicago prairie - it is a modern planting in DuPage County, 50 km west of the scene, and the flora dataset is sourced from the plant lists, not from this frame
anything about 1835. It is a modern physical analogue used for calibration; its tier is a placement on this project's evidence scale, not a claim that it testifies to the scene date
